units.translation: a much-lamented life, enduring the pitiful blood of her dear citizens.
How then were you unharmed by the wrath of Loxias?
May this matter be without harm to the strangers.
so that these things may be accomplished without harm.
Thus I wrote for μὴ ἀνατραπῆναι [not to be overturned].
This man caused the city of the Cadmeans to be overturned.
lest great wealth (a divinity, according to Heimsoeth) having stirred up the dust overturn prosperity with its foot.
nourishing nothing in the light (fear, according to Auratus) in the heart (the scholiast seems to have read 'in the light of the heart').
For I chose the overturnings of the house.
Scholiast: τῷ ἀναύδῳ μένει τῶν χαλινῶν τῶν μὴ ἐώντων αὐτὴν λαλεῖν [with the voiceless force of the reins that do not allow her to speak].
The dust in the air, appearing, persuades me, a voiceless, clear, true messenger.
I see dust, a voiceless messenger of the army.
They are torn by the sea, by the voiceless children (i.e., fish) of the undefiled one.
neither voiceless nor kindling a flame for you.
who, like a tunny, endured without groaning, voiceless.
with the voiceless force of the reins.
with the voiceless force of the reins that do not allow her to speak
i.e., ships that are no longer ships: where, having deleted the second avaeç, I added oloî.
The three-banked ships perished, ships without ships, without ships.
The reading is uncertain, nor is Hermann's conjecture at Ch. 815 ἀμφανεῖ [to reveal] for ἄλλα φανεῖ [other things will appear] more certain.
The one who harms is revealed.
i.e., this too happens to us because of that murder, as Hermann explains. ἂν φέρειν [to bring] Turnebus, αὖ φέρειν [to bring again] Blomfield.
They brought libations more ready for laughter.
And this burden, dripping with blood, would be brought upon us by the murder.
They send, kindling the great beard of flame.
the things — were broken from above upon those sitting man by man.
Should you not have banished this man from this land?
He banished his brother from the city and from his home.
I say that you are not justly banishing Orestes.
to punish this same man in the same way, as a banisher into exile.

ἀνδρόβουλος γυνή [a woman with manly counsel] in Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 19, 23 perhaps from this passage. Similar is what Hesychius noted: ἀνδρολήμην [man-spirited] (correctly ἀνδρόλημον [man-spirited] according to Meineke Philol. vol. 13 p. 516): ἀνδρὸς ἔχουσαν λῆμα [having the spirit of a man].
expecting the manly-counselling heart of a woman.
having the spirit of a man
